title: Machiavelli: Power Without Illusions
subtitle: What politics looks like when you describe it as it is, not as it ought to be
objectives: By the end you will be able to place Machiavelli in the turbulent politics of Renaissance Florence.
Explain his key concepts of virtù and fortuna and his famous claim that it is safer to be feared than loved.
Describe how the Discourses on Livy complicates the picture of Machiavelli as a mere adviser to tyrants.
Define political realism and assess the major interpretations and criticisms of Machiavelli.
Apply Machiavellian analysis to a modern political or organizational situation.
hook:
In December 1513 a former civil servant wrote a letter to a friend in Rome. He had recently been arrested, accused of plotting against the Medici family who now ruled his city, and tortured with the *strappado*, in which a prisoner's wrists were tied behind his back and he was hoisted into the air by them. Released under an amnesty, he had retreated in disgrace to a small farm outside Florence.

In the letter he describes his days: snaring birds, chatting with woodcutters, playing cards and arguing in the local inn. But in the evening, he says, he goes home, takes off his muddy everyday clothes, puts on the robes he wore at court, and enters the ancient courts of the great men of antiquity. There he speaks with them and asks them the reasons for their actions, and they answer him. For four hours, he says, he feels no boredom and forgets every trouble. From those conversations he has composed a little work on principalities.

The man was Niccolò Machiavelli. The little work was *The Prince*. Five centuries later his name is an adjective for cunning manipulation. Was he a teacher of evil, a patriot, a satirist, or simply the first person honest enough to describe how power actually works?

sections.heading: Florence: A City of Plots, Preachers and Invasions
sections.body:
To understand Machiavelli you need to picture Italy around 1500. There was no unified Italian state. The peninsula was a patchwork of city-states, kingdoms and papal territories: Venice, Milan, Florence, Naples, the Papal States and many smaller lordships. They fought each other constantly, often using **mercenaries**, professional soldiers who fought for pay and were notoriously unreliable. From 1494, the great powers of France and Spain invaded repeatedly, using Italy as a battlefield.

Florence itself lurched from one regime to another. For much of the fifteenth century the Medici banking family dominated the city behind a republican facade. In 1494 they were expelled, and the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola led a fiery religious republic, complete with the “bonfire of the vanities,” until he was executed in 1498. Machiavelli later remarked in *The Prince* that Savonarola failed because he was an unarmed prophet; all armed prophets have conquered and the unarmed ones have come to ruin.

In 1498, aged twenty-nine, **Niccolò Machiavelli** (1469–1527) became secretary of the Second Chancery of the Florentine republic, a senior civil service post handling foreign affairs and war. For fourteen years he went on diplomatic missions to the King of France, the Holy Roman Emperor, the Pope and, most memorably, Cesare Borgia. He watched powerful people up close. He also organized a Florentine citizen militia, believing that a state should not depend on hired soldiers.

In 1512 the militia was routed by Spanish troops, the republic fell and the Medici returned. Machiavelli lost his job, was imprisoned and tortured, and retired to his farm. *The Prince* (written in 1513, published only in 1532, five years after his death) was partly a job application, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici in hope of employment. It did not get him the job he hoped for.

sections.heading: The Break: How People Live, Not How They Ought to Live
sections.body:
Many writers before Machiavelli had written “mirrors for princes,” advice books telling rulers to be just, merciful, generous and pious, like Erasmus' *Education of a Christian Prince* (1516). Machiavelli deliberately breaks with this tradition. In chapter 15 of *The Prince* he says that many have imagined republics and principalities that have never been seen or known to exist in truth. But the gap between how people live and how they ought to live is so great that anyone who neglects what is done for what ought to be done learns his ruin rather than his preservation. A person who wants to be good in every way will come to ruin among so many who are not good.

Hence his most notorious advice: a prince who wishes to maintain himself must learn to be able *not* to be good, and to use this or not according to necessity.

This is the birth of what we now call **political realism**: the view that politics should be analyzed in terms of power, interests and consequences as they actually operate, rather than in terms of ideal moral standards. Notice how different this is from Plato's *Republic* (Days 13–14), which designed the perfect city in thought, or from Aquinas' natural law (Day 36), which held that a human law contrary to moral law is no true law. Machiavelli is asking a different question: not “What is the just state?” but “How does someone gain, keep and lose power?”

His method is that of a humanist (Day 38): study history, especially Roman history, and recent events, and draw general lessons from them. He treats politics almost like a craft or a science, with cases, patterns and rules of thumb.

sections.heading: Virtù and Fortuna
sections.body:
Two Italian words are the keys to Machiavelli's thinking.

**Fortuna** is fortune, chance, the unpredictable course of events. Remember Boethius' Lady Philosophy and her wheel of fortune (Day 31)? For Boethius, the wise person accepts Fortune's turns and looks to eternal goods. Machiavelli's response is far more combative. In chapter 25 he estimates that fortune is the arbiter of perhaps half of our actions, but leaves the other half, or close to it, for us to govern. He compares fortune to a raging river that floods the plains, uproots trees and carries away buildings. We cannot stop the flood once it comes, but in calm times we can build dikes and embankments so that next time the damage will be limited. In a notorious image that reflects the sexism of his time, he also says fortune is a woman who favors the bold and the young.

**Virtù** is the quality that lets a person master fortune. It is *not* the same as moral virtue, though the word comes from the Latin *virtus*, manliness or excellence. Machiavellian virtù is a mix of energy, courage, foresight, adaptability and ruthless decisiveness: the ability to read a situation and do what it requires. A ruler with virtù builds the dikes before the flood.

Machiavelli's favorite contemporary example was **Cesare Borgia**, son of Pope Alexander VI, who carved out a state in the Romagna region. Machiavelli tells how Borgia appointed a cruel deputy, Remirro de Orco, to pacify the lawless region. When the deputy's harshness had restored order but made him hated, Borgia had him cut in two and left in the town square of Cesena one morning, a spectacle, Machiavelli says, that left the people at once satisfied and stunned. The cruelty was useful, and the blame went to someone else. Borgia ultimately failed, partly through bad luck when his father died and he himself fell ill at the same moment. Even great virtù cannot master fortune completely.

Machiavelli also distinguishes cruelty well used from cruelty badly used. Well-used cruelty, if one may speak well of evil, he says, is done all at once out of necessity and then turned to the subjects' benefit; badly used cruelty grows over time. Injuries should be done all together, benefits given little by little.

sections.heading: Feared or Loved? Lions, Foxes and Appearances
sections.body:
Chapter 17 asks whether it is better for a prince to be loved or feared. Ideally, both. But since it is difficult to combine them, it is much safer to be feared than loved, if one must be lacking. Why? Because people, Machiavelli says, are generally ungrateful, fickle, deceitful, cowardly and greedy. While you benefit them they are entirely yours, but when danger approaches they turn away. Love is held by a chain of obligation that people break whenever it suits them; fear is held by dread of punishment, which never fails.

But notice the crucial qualification that is often forgotten: a prince must avoid being **hated**. He can achieve this by keeping his hands off his citizens' property and their women. People, Machiavelli adds, forget the death of a father more quickly than the loss of their inheritance.

Chapter 18 asks whether princes must keep their word. Machiavelli's answer: a wise ruler cannot and should not keep faith when doing so would work against him and the reasons that made him promise no longer exist. If all people were good, this would be bad advice, but since they are wicked and would not keep faith with you, you need not keep it with them. A prince must know how to use both the beast and the man, and among the beasts he should imitate the **lion and the fox**: the lion cannot defend itself from traps, and the fox cannot defend itself from wolves. One must be a fox to recognize traps and a lion to frighten wolves.

Above all, a prince must *seem* merciful, faithful, humane, honest and religious, and even be so, while remaining ready to act otherwise when necessary. Most people judge by appearances and by results. Everyone sees what you appear to be; few touch what you are.

This is the core of the reputation that gave us the word **Machiavellian**, meaning cunning, manipulative and willing to do anything for advantage. Shakespeare could already have a character boast that he could set “the murderous Machiavel to school.” But is that the whole Machiavelli?

sections.heading: The Other Machiavelli: The Discourses and the Republic
sections.body:
Alongside *The Prince*, Machiavelli worked on a much longer book, the *Discourses on the First Ten Books of Titus Livy* (written c. 1513–1519, published 1531). Livy was the Roman historian of the early republic. In the *Discourses*, Machiavelli emerges as a passionate **republican**: a believer in self-governing states in which citizens share power.

He argues that republics, when well ordered, are more stable and more successful than principalities, because they can draw on a diversity of citizens whose different talents suit different times. He praises the Roman people and says that, on the whole, the people are wiser and more constant than a prince. Most strikingly, he argues that the conflicts between Rome's nobles and common people, which others saw as a weakness, were actually the cause of Roman liberty, because they produced laws and institutions protecting freedom. Healthy politics, on this view, channels conflict rather than eliminating it.

The *Discourses* also insist on **civic virtue**: citizens' willingness to put the common good ahead of private interests, defend the state with their own arms and obey the laws. Religion matters here too, but in a striking way. Machiavelli admired how Roman religion bound citizens to their oaths and to the state, and he complained that Christianity, as then interpreted, glorified humble and contemplative people rather than people of action, making the world weak.

So how do the two books fit together? Scholars disagree:

- Some see no contradiction: *The Prince* is about founding or rescuing a state in a crisis, when a single strong hand is needed; the *Discourses* are about maintaining liberty once it exists.
- Some see *The Prince* as a job application and the *Discourses* as Machiavelli's real view.
- A few readers, including Rousseau (Day 53), suggested *The Prince* was secretly a satire or a warning to the people, exposing how tyrants really operate. Most modern scholars find this reading strained, but it shows how puzzling the book is.

The last chapter of *The Prince* adds another twist: a passionate plea for a redeemer to unite Italy and free it from foreign “barbarians.” Behind the cold advice stands a patriot.

sections.heading: Teacher of Evil or Founder of Political Science?
sections.body:
Machiavelli's legacy is fought over to this day. Here are the main interpretations.

1. **The teacher of evil.** The political philosopher Leo Strauss called Machiavelli a teacher of evil, arguing that he consciously set out to overturn classical and Christian morality and found a new, purely worldly politics. The Catholic Church placed his works on its Index of forbidden books in 1559.
2. **The scientist of politics.** Others see him as the founder of a value-neutral political science, who simply described how power operates, the way a doctor describes a disease without endorsing it.
3. **The pluralist.** The philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in a famous essay “The Originality of Machiavelli,” argued that Machiavelli did not reject morality but revealed that there are two incompatible moralities: Christian virtues of humility and mercy, and pagan, civic virtues of glory and the strength of the state. One cannot have both fully, and choosing between them has a real cost. This, for Berlin, was Machiavelli's deeply unsettling discovery.
4. **The republican.** Historians such as Quentin Skinner and J. G. A. Pocock have placed Machiavelli in a tradition of civic republicanism stretching from Rome to the American founders.

Whatever interpretation you prefer, Machiavelli raises the problem of **dirty hands**: can it be right, or even required, for a political leader to do something morally wrong for the sake of the community? Think of a leader who lies to prevent a panic or authorizes a violent act to prevent a greater disaster. Machiavelli's answer is that a leader who refuses ever to dirty his hands may doom the people who depend on him.

Critics answer that once leaders give themselves permission to deceive and kill “when necessary,” necessity has a way of appearing everywhere. Note too Machiavelli's dark picture of human nature. On Day 42, Thomas Hobbes will build a whole political theory on a similar pessimism.

keyQuote.text: It is necessary to a prince, if he wants to maintain himself, to learn to be able not to be good, and to use this and not use it according to necessity.
keyQuote.source: Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter 15 (trans. Harvey C. Mansfield)

modernConnection.title: Realpolitik, Spin Doctors and the Office Machiavelli
modernConnection.body:
Machiavelli's ideas are everywhere in modern life, sometimes under other names.

In international relations, the **realist** school, associated with thinkers like Hans Morgenthau and practitioners like Henry Kissinger, holds that states act primarily to secure power and survival, and that foreign policy built on moral crusades is naive and dangerous. When a democracy allies with an unsavory regime because it shares a common enemy, or keeps silent about human rights abuses to secure trade or energy supplies, it is acting in a Machiavellian spirit. Critics answer that realism can become a self-fulfilling excuse for cynicism.

In domestic politics, Machiavelli's insight that people judge by appearances and results anticipates the entire profession of political communications. Image consultants, focus groups, “spin” and carefully staged photo opportunities are about managing what the public sees. The insistence that a leader must seem honest, merciful and religious rather than necessarily be so would not surprise any modern campaign strategist. Note, however, that in modern democracies with a free press, the gap between appearance and reality can be exposed more easily; scandals are often precisely the moment when a leader's appearance collapses.

Psychologists have even turned Machiavelli into a personality measure. In 1970 Richard Christie and Florence Geis published research on “Machiavellianism,” a trait involving manipulativeness, cynicism about human nature and a willingness to deceive. It is now studied as part of the so-called Dark Triad, alongside narcissism and psychopathy. Business books promise Machiavellian lessons for office politics.

But the comparison has limits worth noticing. Machiavelli wrote for a world of armed city-states, mercenaries and assassinations, where losing power often meant losing your life. A manager playing office politics or a candidate managing a brand faces very different stakes. And the personality trait called Machiavellianism is about self-serving manipulation, while Machiavelli himself was often concerned with the survival and glory of the state and, in the Discourses, with the liberty of citizens. Ask, when you see Machiavellian tactics today: in whose service are they used, a person's ambition or a community's survival?

vocabulary.definition: Machiavelli's term for the energy, skill, boldness and adaptability that enable a person to achieve great things and master fortune; not the same as moral virtue.
vocabulary.example: Cesare Borgia showed virtù when he acted swiftly to secure his new territories.

vocabulary.definition: Fortune or chance, the unpredictable force that Machiavelli thought governs about half of human affairs.
vocabulary.example: Machiavelli compared fortuna to a flooding river against which one must build dikes in calm times.

vocabulary.definition: The approach to politics that analyzes power, interests and consequences as they actually operate, rather than starting from ideal moral standards.
vocabulary.example: Political realism asks how a state can survive, not how a perfectly just state would look.

vocabulary.definition: In ordinary usage, cunning, manipulative and willing to use deceit for advantage; a label that oversimplifies Machiavelli himself.
vocabulary.example: The coworker who secretly takes credit for others' work is often called Machiavellian.

vocabulary.definition: The political tradition favoring self-government by citizens under law, mixed institutions and active civic participation, rather than rule by one person.
vocabulary.example: Machiavelli's Discourses on Livy show his republicanism in their praise of Roman liberty.

vocabulary.definition: Citizens' disposition to put the common good above private interest, defend the state and uphold its laws.
vocabulary.example: Machiavelli thought a citizen militia required civic virtue that mercenaries lacked.

vocabulary.definition: The problem of whether political leaders may, or must, commit moral wrongs to secure important public goods.
vocabulary.example: A leader who lies to prevent a deadly panic faces the problem of dirty hands.

vocabulary.definition: A soldier who fights for pay rather than loyalty to a state; Machiavelli considered mercenaries useless and dangerous.
vocabulary.example: Machiavelli blamed Italy's weakness partly on its reliance on mercenary armies.

thinkingExercise.title: Advise the Prince, Then Judge Yourself
thinkingExercise.prompt: Choose a real or realistic situation in which a leader faces a hard choice, for example a mayor during a natural disaster, a CEO facing a scandal, a head of state negotiating with a hostile power, or the leader of a club or team in conflict. You will write two short pieces of advice and then judge them.
steps: Describe the situation in three or four sentences: who holds power, what threatens them, and what is at stake for other people.
Write a short memo of advice in Machiavelli's voice. Use at least two of his ideas (virtù, fortuna, feared rather than loved but never hated, lion and fox, appearances).
Now write a memo in the voice of Erasmus or Aquinas, who believed rulers must be good in fact, not only in appearance.

Which memo would actually lead to a better outcome for the people affected, and which would you feel comfortable having your name on? If your answers differ, explain what that tells you about the problem of dirty hands.

summary: Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat whose career ended when the Medici returned in 1512; he wrote The Prince in 1513 while in forced retirement.
He broke with the mirror-for-princes tradition by describing how rulers actually gain and keep power, founding what we now call political realism.
Virtù, energetic and adaptable skill, allows a ruler to master fortuna, the chance that governs about half of human affairs.
It is safer to be feared than loved if one cannot be both, but a ruler must avoid being hated; he must combine lion and fox and manage appearances.
The Discourses on Livy reveal a passionate republican, and interpreters still debate whether Machiavelli was a teacher of evil, a scientist of power, a pluralist or a patriot.

quiz.question: What was Machiavelli's situation when he wrote The Prince in 1513?
options: He was ruling Florence as its prince
He had lost his government post after the Medici returned and had been imprisoned and tortured
He was a cardinal in Rome
He was a professor at the University of Paris
quiz.explanation: Machiavelli served the Florentine republic from 1498 until its fall in 1512; afterward he was arrested, tortured and retired to his farm, where he wrote The Prince.

quiz.question: In chapter 15 of The Prince, Machiavelli breaks with earlier advice books by:
options: Insisting rulers must imitate Christ
Designing an ideal republic
Focusing on what people actually do rather than what they ought to do
Arguing that politics should be left to philosophers
quiz.explanation: He says that those who ignore how people actually live, for the sake of how they ought to live, bring about their own ruin.

quiz.question: What does Machiavelli mean by virtù?
options: Energy, skill, boldness and adaptability in mastering circumstances
Christian humility and charity
Sexual purity
Strict obedience to law in all cases
quiz.explanation: Virtù is excellence in action, not moral virtue; it can even include well-used cruelty and deception.

quiz.question: Machiavelli compares fortuna to a river in flood. What lesson does he draw?
options: Nothing can be done against fortune, so accept it calmly
Fortune always favors the virtuous
Fortune can be completely controlled by prayer
In calm times we should build dikes and embankments to limit future damage
quiz.explanation: Fortune governs about half our affairs, but foresight in quiet times can limit its damage, a contrast with Boethius' acceptance.

quiz.question: Machiavelli said a prince should try to be hated, since hatred is a strong form of fear.
quiz.explanation: He said it is safer to be feared than loved if one must choose, but a prince must avoid being hated, especially by respecting subjects' property and women.

quiz.question: Why should a prince imitate both the lion and the fox?
options: Because both are symbols of Florence
Because the lion cannot recognize traps and the fox cannot frighten wolves, so a ruler needs both cunning and force
Because animals are morally superior to humans
Because they represent loyalty and patience
quiz.explanation: Chapter 18 argues a ruler needs the fox's cunning to spot traps and the lion's strength to scare off enemies.

quiz.question: In the Discourses on Livy, Machiavelli argues that conflicts between Rome's nobles and common people helped produce Roman liberty.
quiz.explanation: He held that well-channeled conflict produced laws protecting freedom, a sign of his republican commitments.

quiz.question: Isaiah Berlin's interpretation of Machiavelli holds that:
options: Machiavelli was secretly a devout Christian
The Prince is purely a satire
Machiavelli revealed two incompatible moralities, Christian and civic-pagan, between which we must choose at a cost
Machiavelli had no interest in morality at all
quiz.explanation: Berlin saw Machiavelli as uncovering a clash of values, not simply rejecting ethics.

quiz.question: A government allies with an authoritarian regime it dislikes because both oppose a more dangerous common enemy. This is best described as:
options: Natural law reasoning
Negative theology
Utopian idealism
Political realism
quiz.explanation: Putting power and survival above moral approval of one's partners is the hallmark of political realism, which descends from Machiavelli.

quiz.question: The Prince was published during Machiavelli's lifetime and immediately won him a high post under the Medici.
quiz.explanation: The Prince circulated in manuscript and was printed only in 1532, five years after his death; it did not win him the employment he sought.

goDeeper.body:
The problem of dirty hands received its classic modern statement in the political theorist Michael Walzer's 1973 essay “Political Action: The Problem of Dirty Hands.” Walzer imagines a politician who, to win an election and do much good, must make a corrupt deal, or a leader who orders the torture of a captured terrorist to locate bombs about to explode. Walzer argues that such a leader may be right to act and yet still be guilty: we would not want a leader who refused to dirty his hands, but neither would we want one who felt no guilt. The moral remainder does not vanish just because the act was justified. This is close to Berlin's reading of Machiavelli and very far from simple consequentialism.

A second scholarly frontier concerns Machiavelli's republicanism. The so-called Cambridge School of intellectual history, especially Quentin Skinner and J. G. A. Pocock, argued that Machiavelli belongs to a long tradition of thinking about liberty as non-domination: being free means not living under the arbitrary power of another, which requires active, armed and vigilant citizens. Pocock's *The Machiavellian Moment* traced this idea through seventeenth-century England to the American Revolution. More recently, John McCormick has argued in *Machiavellian Democracy* that Machiavelli was even more populist than usually thought, favoring institutions that let ordinary citizens check elites.

Finally, a puzzle to ponder: if Machiavelli was right that a successful prince must hide his methods, why did Machiavelli publish them? Some readers think that exposing the methods was itself a political act, educating the many about how they are ruled.

readings.author: Niccolò Machiavelli (trans. Harvey C. Mansfield or George Bull)
readings.note: Short and readable; focus on chapters 15–18, 25 and 26.

readings.note: A leading historian places Machiavelli in his humanist and republican context.

readings.author: Isaiah Berlin
readings.note: Classic essay, collected in Against the Current, arguing that Machiavelli revealed a clash of incompatible values.

readings.author: Niccolò Machiavelli

questions: Can a political leader be a good person and a good leader at the same time? Under what conditions might these come apart?
Is it better for a leader to be feared or loved in a modern democracy? Has the answer changed since Machiavelli's day?
Is describing how power works neutral, or does it inevitably teach people how to abuse it?
